const express = require('express');
const app = express();

function rateLimiter(maxRequests, timeWindowInSeconds) {
  const clientRequestData = new Map();

  return (req, res, next) => {
    const clientIP = req.ip;

    if (!clientRequestData.has(clientIP)) {
      clientRequestData.set(clientIP, { requests: 1, timestamp: Date.now() });
      return next();
    }

    const requestData = clientRequestData.get(clientIP);
    const currentTime = Date.now();
    const timeDifference = (currentTime - requestData.timestamp) / 1000;

    if (timeDifference < timeWindowInSeconds) {
      if (requestData.requests < maxRequests) {
        requestData.requests += 1;
        return next();
      } else {
        res.status(429).json({ message: 'Too Many Requests' });
      }
    } else {
      clientRequestData.set(clientIP, { requests: 1, timestamp: Date.now() });
      return next();
    }
  };

Arduino lib layout: A guide for new contributors

If you're a new contributor to an Arduino C++ library project, you might be wondering how the library is laid out and what files are required. In this guide, we'll answer some common questions about Arduino lib layout to help you get started.

Library.properties file

One of the most important files in an Arduino library is the library.properties file. This file contains metadata about the library, including its name, version number, author, and description. This information is used by the Arduino IDE and other tools to help users find and install the library.

More information

If you want to learn more about library.properties and how to create it, you can check out the official Arduino documentation at https://arduino.github.io/arduino-cli/latest/library-specification/#library-properties-file. This page also covers other aspects of the library specification, such as the directory structure and file naming conventions.

Compiled and copied files

When you compile an Arduino sketch that uses a library, the library code is compiled along with the sketch code into a single binary file. However, not all files in the library directory are compiled. Files with extensions like .h, .hpp, and .cpp are compiled, but other files like documentation and examples are not. These files are simply copied to the final sketch directory.

Public and private headers

In an Arduino library, some header files are intended to be used by external code and are considered "public," while others are only used internally and are considered "private" or "internal." Typically, public headers are placed in the library's root directory, while private headers are placed in a subdirectory called "src."

Testing code

If you want to test code that's supposed to run on an Arduino, you'll need to set up a development environment that emulates an Arduino board. This can be done using tools like the Arduino Simulator or the PlatformIO simulator. You can also use real Arduino boards for testing, but this can be more time-consuming and expensive.

Compatibility with PlatformIO

If you're using PlatformIO, you'll be happy to know that library.properties is fully compatible with PlatformIO's library specification. This means that you can easily publish your library to both the Arduino Library Manager and the PlatformIO Library Registry.

Required files

At a minimum, an Arduino library needs two files: a header file (with extension .h or .hpp) that defines the library's public interface, and a source file (with extension .cpp) that implements the library's functionality. However, you'll typically want to include additional files like documentation, examples, and a library.properties file.

Publishing a library

To publish an Arduino library, you'll need to create a GitHub repository for the library and upload the required files. Once you've done that, you can submit your library to the Arduino Library Manager for inclusion in the official Arduino library repository. You can also publish your library to the PlatformIO Library Registry.

Naming convention

When naming your library, it's important to follow the Arduino library naming convention. This convention states that library names should be short and descriptive, with words separated by underscores. For example, "WiFi101" and "LiquidCrystal_I2C" are both valid library names.

Code conventions

Finally, it's worth noting that there are no specific code conventions that all Arduino libraries must follow. However, it's generally a good idea to follow standard C++ coding conventions, such as using namespaces and avoiding global variables. While it is true that observational data can be collected in real-world settings without manipulating any variables, using observational data to test the effectiveness of a marketing campaign has several limitations. Here are some counterarguments to your colleague’s argument:

  1. Lacking a control group: In observational studies, there is no control group, which makes it difficult to isolate the effect of the marketing campaign from other factors that may influence the outcome. Without a control group, it is challenging to determine whether any observed changes in behavior or sales are actually due to the marketing campaign.

  2. Biases and confounding factors: Observational data can be biased because factors other than the marketing campaign may influence the outcome. For example, the demographics of the customers, the time of day, or the weather can all affect sales, making it difficult to attribute any changes to the marketing campaign. In contrast, experimental methods can control for confounding factors by randomly assigning participants to treatment and control groups.

  3. No causality: Observational studies can show correlation but not causality. Correlation does not necessarily mean causation, and it can be difficult to infer a cause-and-effect relationship between the marketing campaign and the outcome without experimental methods.

  4. Limited generalizability: Observational data is collected in a particular setting, making it difficult to generalize the results to other contexts. In contrast, experimental methods allow for more control over the setting, making it easier to replicate the results in other settings.

  5. Difficulty measuring ROI: Observational data can make it difficult to measure the return on investment (ROI) of the marketing campaign accurately. Without a control group, it is challenging to isolate the effect of the marketing campaign from other factors that may influence the outcome, making it difficult to calculate the ROI accurately.

Overall, while observational data can be useful for exploratory analyses, experimental methods are more robust and reliable when it comes to testing the effectiveness of a marketing campaign.

A natural experiment is a situation where an event or intervention occurs naturally, providing researchers with an opportunity to observe the effects of the intervention without manipulating it. For example, the introduction of a new law or policy can be considered a natural experiment. Researchers can compare outcomes before and after the intervention and compare them with a control group to estimate the causal effect of the intervention.

Instrumental variables are another technique used to infer causality from observational data. An instrumental variable is a variable that affects the outcome only through its effect on the treatment variable. The use of an instrumental variable can help overcome the problem of unobserved confounding variables that can bias estimates of causal effects. For example, if a researcher wants to estimate the effect of a marketing campaign on sales, but there are unobserved factors that affect both the campaign and sales, the researcher can use an instrumental variable, such as the price of a related product, to isolate the effect of the campaign on sales.

However, experimental methods are still generally considered more robust for testing causality, as they provide a more controlled environment for observing the effects of a particular intervention or treatment.

The regression discontinuity design works by exploiting a discontinuity in the assignment of participants to treatment or control groups based on a specific threshold or cutoff point. Participants who fall on one side of the cutoff point receive the treatment, while those who fall on the other side do not. Tailwind's classes are organized into categories such as typography, colors, spacing, and layout. You can customize the framework by editing its configuration file, which allows you to add, modify or remove classes. This gives you a great deal of flexibility while still allowing you to maintain consistency in your design.

When you use Tailwind, your HTML markup tends to be more verbose, with a higher number of classes used to describe the desired design. This approach can take some time to get used to, but it offers the advantage of faster development time and more consistent styling. By using pre-built classes, you avoid writing custom CSS, which can be error-prone and time-consuming.

Overall, Tailwind CSS is a powerful and flexible framework that can help you create responsive, consistent designs quickly and efficiently.
